claims.text: Suitable high-temperature processing produces a selective, continuous spinel-type oxide film on at least one phase of the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Surface enrichment in Al and Fe is responsible for formation of the spinel-type oxide film.
Mechanical wear removes or microcracks the protective oxide layer.
The intact oxide layer impedes aggressive ions and protects the underlying alloy.
Wear-induced oxide damage exposes an underlying phase or surface that is less corrosion resistant.
Exposure of the less-stable phase triggers localized galvanic corrosion at phase interfaces.
Localized corrosion further weakens oxide and surface integrity, thereby promoting additional wear.
Mutually reinforcing oxide removal, galvanic corrosion, and additional wear form a positive feedback loop that accelerates coupled degradation.
Coarser phase segregation leads to more discontinuous oxide coverage.
Relative to a matched baseline with a continuous and adherent oxide film, the variant with disrupted oxide coverage will have a higher total degradation rate.
The disrupted-oxide variant will exhibit a higher corrosion current density than the continuous-oxide baseline.
The disrupted-oxide variant will exhibit greater wear mass loss than the continuous-oxide baseline.
Repeated oxide removal enhances the wear rate.
The proposed feedback operates near 900 °C in chloride-containing conditions when the mechanical load disrupts surface films without causing immediate gross failure.
Reciprocating wear testing of a high-entropy alloy can be performed at 900 °C.
The controlled comparison uses otherwise identically tested samples with robust continuous oxide coverage versus samples with discontinuous oxide coverage.

Failure to observe higher wear mass loss and corrosion current density in the disrupted-oxide samples, or failure to observe a correlation between oxide integrity and degradation, falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The experiment specifies a 3.5 wt% NaCl aqueous solution at approximately 900 °C without defining the pressure or a molten/salt-deposit alternative. An ordinary aqueous solution cannot be maintained at that temperature, so the stated thermal and environmental boundary conditions are not jointly defined.
